meta.title: BlackBerry Ran Half of America's Smartphones. Then It Didn't.
meta.hook: BlackBerry's own filings explain its collapse in one sentence: customers wanted products and apps it did not yet have.
meta.description: BlackBerry-maker RIM held around 50% of the US smartphone market and peaked near 85 million subscribers worldwide in 2011, four years after the iPhone launched. By 2012 its global smartphone share had collapsed to under 5%. The company kept betting on physical keyboards and enterprise email while the market moved to touchscreens and app ecosystems. Educational content only, not financial advice.

scenes.narration: BlackBerry's own filings explain its collapse in one sentence: customers wanted products and apps it did not yet have.

visual.query: old blackberry phone physical keyboard close up
visual.visual_intent: Macro shot of a BlackBerry's physical keyboard under warm office light, thumbs typing fast
visual.decision_reason: hook beat: the peak stat, RIM ~50% US share/~85M subscribers 2011, hard cut

scenes.narration: The company had built enormous loyalty around secure messaging, enterprise email, and its physical keyboard.

visual.visual_intent: A modern touchscreen phone being scrolled by hand, smooth glass, contrast with the prior keyboard shot
visual.decision_reason: sets the timeline contrast; iPhone launched 2007, widely documented

scenes.narration: But touchscreen competitors changed expectations around browsers, media, and large app ecosystems.

visual.query: businessman typing email phone office desk
visual.visual_intent: A businessman typing intently on a keyboard phone at a desk, corporate confidence, unaware of the shift outside
visual.decision_reason: RIM's continued keyboard/enterprise focus is well documented across multiple business-history retrospectives

scenes.narration: BlackBerry reported intense U.S. competition, delayed product launches, and no timely high-end LTE offering.

visual.query: app icons grid screen colorful smartphone
visual.visual_intent: A colorful grid of app icons filling a smartphone screen, energetic and modern, contrasts the beige enterprise feel before
visual.decision_reason: visualizes the app-ecosystem shift RIM was slow to match

scenes.narration: Its next-generation BlackBerry Ten devices arrived after many consumers and developers had already moved to iPhone or Android.

visual.query: declining bar chart red arrow down screen
visual.visual_intent: A bar chart shrinking dramatically downward on a dark display, sharp red decline arrow
visual.decision_reason: the collapse from ~20% (2009) to <5% (2012) global share, confirmed via Statista-cited retrospectives

scenes.narration: The old strengths never vanished. They simply stopped being enough once the basis of competition changed.

visual.visual_intent: An old keyboard phone sitting unused in a drawer among cables, quiet, closing image of obsolescence
